topic.title: Five words that add 30% to a price
topic.claim: Five words add a third to any price in India: artisanal, handcrafted, small-batch, clean and curated.
topic.moment: A ₹650 jar of 'small-batch' peanut butter next to a ₹250 one with the same two ingredients.

turn.believed: These words describe how the product is made.
turn.actually: They describe how you should feel about paying more.

topic.because: Nobody can check if something is truly small-batch. A word you can't verify is the cheapest story a brand can buy.
topic.payoff: Cover the label and read the ingredients. If they match the cheap one, you were paying for the adjective.
topic.behaviour: Brands lean on unverifiable labels; shoppers pay more for them at cafés and stores.
topic.mechanism: Words that can't be checked make premium pricing cheap to justify.
topic.group: Urban shoppers at premium grocery and café counters
topic.send_to: The friend whose kitchen shelf is all 'artisanal'.
topic.why_now: Gift hampers full of these words are filling the shelves before Diwali.

score.why: Premium is packaging and a story; the artisanal peanut butter shelf is exactly what people see.

cover.headline: Five words that make you [pay more] for the same jar

paragraphs: Five words that make you pay more for the same jar.
It's a Sunday at the fancy grocery store. Soft music, wooden shelves, a basket with a leather handle you didn't ask for.

Two jars of peanut butter. One says *small-batch*, handcrafted and clean in a font that looks handwritten, next to a tiny drawing of a farm. The plain one sits a shelf lower, at a much friendlier price.
slides.why_swipe: You already know which one you picked.

paragraphs: You don't turn either one around. The front has already done its job.
The pricey one goes in the basket. It looks like what someone with their life sorted spreads on sourdough, standing at a clean kitchen counter.
slides.why_swipe: So what did the extra money actually buy?

paragraphs: In that aisle, you can't check how small a batch is, or whose hands did the crafting.
**These words don't describe the peanuts. They describe how you should feel at the billing counter.**
A word you can't check is the cheapest story a brand can buy. A nicer font costs them very little. It adds rupees to every single jar.
slides.why_swipe: So is every fancy label a con?

paragraphs: To be fair, some makers really are one small kitchen and one grinder. For them, the word is true.
But it costs the same to print for everyone else. So this month the Diwali hamper at your door says curated on the box and artisanal on the ribbon.
**Nobody flips a gift over to read the back. That's where these words earn the most.**
slides.why_swipe: So what was inside the jar all along?

paragraphs: The fancy jar runs out midweek. The corner shop only has the plain one, so that comes home. Before the empty one gets washed for storing dal, both sit side by side.
You flip them. Peanuts, salt. Peanuts, salt. **The extra money bought you one adjective.**

end.save: Same ingredients, higher price: that's an adjective you paid for.
end.send: The friend whose kitchen shelf is all 'artisanal'.

draft.caption: Which 'artisanal' thing in your kitchen turned out to have the exact same ingredients as the cheap one?
draft.alt_text: Carousel about premium labels in India. A shopper at a fancy grocery store picks a pricey peanut butter jar labelled small-batch, handcrafted and clean in a handwritten-style font over a cheaper plain jar, without reading the back. The post argues these words can't be checked, so they sell a feeling about paying more rather than describing the product, which makes them a cheap story for brands. It grants that some small makers use them truthfully, and notes that Diwali hampers labelled curated and artisanal get away with it most because nobody checks a gift. Later the shopper ends up with the plain jar too, flips both and finds the same two ingredients, peanuts and salt. The extra money bought one adjective.
